1:1: In this title for the book, the term word refers to the message that the Lord sent to the Judeans through Zephaniah by using words.
The words Zephaniah, Cushi, Gedaliah, Amariah, Hezekiah, Josiah, and Amon are the names of men.
In this title, the term days means a specific time, the reign of Josiah as king of Judah.
1:2: אָסֹף אָסֵף כֹּל מֵעַל פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה

When the Lord says that he is going to destroy everything on the surface of the earth, he is probably making an overstatement for emphasis. He wants to express how angry he is at the sinful disobedience of people.
The Lord is speaking as if the surface of the earth or ground were literally its face.
1:3: אָסֵף אָדָם וּבְהֵמָה אָסֵף עוֹף־הַשָּׁמַיִם וּדְגֵי הַיָּם
The Lord is using creatures from the three components of creation—land creatures, sky creatures, and sea creatures—to mean all creatures throughout creation.
The Lord is using two types of creatures that live on the earth, man and beast, to mean all creatures that live on the earth.
The Lord is speaking of idols as if they were literally stumbling blocks, that is, objects that people would trip over. He is using stumbling to mean doing what is morally and spiritually wrong.

The implication is that the wicked people the Lord is talking about are doing things that are morally and spiritually wrong because their actions are being guided by the values implicit in idolatry rather than by the Lord’s law.
When the Lord says that he will kill all the people who live on earth, as in verse 2, he is making an overstatement for emphasis.
The Lord is speaking as if he were going to cut off the people who live on the earth the way one would cut a branch off from a tree.
1:4: Here, hand represents the power that a person has to do something.
As the introduction to this chapter discusses, this phrase is the beginning of a litany.
The Lord is using the name Baal by association to mean the worship of Baal, a false god.

The worship of Baal had not been reduced to a remnant at this time. As the introduction to Zephaniah explains, the prophet spoke these oracles to warn the people of Judah that they needed to stop worshiping Baal. So the Lord is using this expression to mean that he will destroy Baal worship so completely that nothing is left—there will be no remnant.

Here, name represents the reputation of an individual, which extends beyond the place and time in which that individual is known personally. When someone’s name in this sense is destroyed, no one remembers that person any longer.

The term priests probably refers to the priests descended from Aaron who were supposed to lead the Israelites in the worship of the Lord. Unfortunately, at this time they were not serving the Lord faithfully, as Zephaniah says in 3:4.
1:5: The Lord is using one aspect of worship, bowing down, to mean worship generally.
The Lord is speaking of the sun, moon, and stars as if they were an army in the skies.

The terms bowing down and swearing to mean similar things. They both indicate worship; bowing down, one aspect of worship, represents worship generally, while the expression swearing to describes pledging oneself to worship the Lord as God. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis since, as the rest of the verse shows, this worship was not wholehearted.
The word translated their king could be the name of a false god, Milcom, also called Molech, Molek, or Moloch.

The Lord is drawing a contrast between swearing to and swearing by. The Judeans who swore to the Lord pledged themselves to worship him as their God. But they then swore by Milcom, invoking the name of that false god to guarantee a vow or promise that they had made. The Lord is saying how inconsistent and inappropriate it was for them to do that.
1:6: The Lord is speaking as if the Judeans who are ceasing to worship him were literally walking on a path and turning back from the direction in which they had been heading.

The Lord could be using the expressions search for and seek to mean: (1) two similar things. He could be speaking as if the Judeans should literally have been looking for him, meaning that they should have been praying to him. In this case the Lord would be using two similar terms together for emphasis. The expression search for could mean to ask for help, and the expression seek could mean to ask for guidance.
1:7: Here the word face represents the presence of a person by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.
The expression the day of the Lord refers to a specific time when God will punish people for their sins.

Zephaniah is speaking as if the Lord had literally prepared a sacrifice and ceremonially cleansed (sanctified) those he had invited to share a meal from the meat of the sacrificed animal. He is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were this sacrifice, and of an enemy army, most likely that of the Babylonians, as if it would feast on the Judeans, meaning that this foreign power would conquer them and plunder them, as verses 13–16 indicate.
1:8: As the introduction to this chapter discusses, this phrase is the beginning of a litany.
As Zephaniah did in the previous verse, the Lord is speaking as if he is literally going to offer a sacrifice.
וּפָקַדְתִּי עַל־הַשָּׂרִים וְעַל־בְּנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְעַל כָּל־הַלֹּבְשִׁים מַלְבּוּשׁ נָכְרִי
The expression visit upon means to punish.
In some languages the term princes describes male direct descendants of a monarch, but here it means court officials who may or may not have been members of the royal family.

This could mean: (1) the actual members of the royal family. In that case, the word sons would have a generic sense, applying to both men and women, and it would mean not just the literal children of the present king but also the grandchildren and even later descendants of previous kings; (2) the literal sons of the present king, Josiah, who would have been just boys at this time. The implication is that the Lord is going to punish the Judeans so thoroughly that not even children will be spared.

The Lord is using one thing that the Judeans were doing to curry favor with foreign powers, wearing the same clothing that they did, to mean everything that they did to curry favor, especially including worshiping their gods.
1:9: The expression leaping over the threshold seems to refer to people entering other people’s houses forcibly, as if in a rush, in order to seize their possessions by violence or fraud.
The Lord is using the terms violence and fraud by association to mean possessions unlawfully obtained from others by violence or on fraudulent grounds.
1:10: The expression the Fish Gate is the name of one of the gates in the wall of the ancient city of Jerusalem. It may have had that name because there was a fish market just outside this gate.

The word Second is the name of one of the districts in the ancient city of Jerusalem. This district may have had that name because it had been added to the original city. Some translations use a name for it that indicates that.
The Lord is using the term hills by association to mean the settlements on the hills around Jerusalem.
1:11: The word Maktesh is the name of one of the districts in the ancient city of Jerusalem. It seems to have been a place where many goods were bought and sold, and so some translations refer to it with a descriptive phrase rather than with this name.
נִדְמָה כָּל־עַם כְּנַעַן נִכְרְתוּ כָּל־נְטִילֵי כָסֶף
These two phrases mean similar things. The Lord is using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.

In this context, the expression people of Canaan refers to traders, not to those from the Canaanite people group. Many traders were Phoenicians, that is, Canaanites, and that is how the profession got this name, but the reference is to the profession and not to the people group.

The Lord is using the expression the ones weighing silver by association to mean merchants. In this culture, people used silver as money, determining its value by its weight. So merchants would weigh silver in order to determine how much of it to pay for goods or to accept in payment for them.
1:12: The Lord is speaking as if he is literally going to use lamps in order to search for evildoers so that he can find them and punish them. He means that he is going to search thoroughly, as if using a lamp in order to see into all dark corners where someone or something might escape notice.

The Lord is speaking as if the sinful, complacent people of Jerusalem were literally wine that is thickening because it has been left on its sediment. The term “sediment” describes the small pieces of stem, leaves, and seeds from grape plants that are unintentionally mixed with the juice during the winemaking process. Ordinarily, these are allowed to settle to the bottom of the wine, which is then poured off to separate it from them. The Lord means that just as wine left on its sediment becomes thick, so these Judeans have become difficult to motivate to repentance.
By do good, these people are implicitly referring to the Lord rewarding them, and by do bad, they are referring to the Lord punishing them.
1:13: The Lord does not mean that these things will happen on their own. He means implicitly that the enemy army he describes in verse 16 will plunder the wealth of these complacent Judeans and ruin their houses.
These words are similar to what the Lord said in (Deuteronomy 28:30).
1:14: The Lord is speaking as if the day or time when he will punish people were a living thing that was hastening to arrive.
The Lord is speaking of the sound of the day by association to mean the sounds that people will make on that day, that is, at that time.
1:15: In these four cases, the Lord is using two words with similar meaning together for emphasis.
יוֹם חֹשֶׁךְ וַאֲפֵלָה יוֹם עָנָן וַעֲרָפֶל

The Lord is speaking as if the sky will literally be dark and cloudy at the time when he punishes people for their sins. He means that it will be a time when people experience much trouble and feel great sorrow.
1:16: The Lord is referring to a ram’s horn, a shofar, that soldiers would use to signal an attack. The Lord is using the term by association to mean the sound that this horn would make.
עַל הֶעָרִים הַבְּצֻרוֹת וְעַל הַפִּנּוֹת הַגְּבֹהוֹת

The Lord is using the term corners by association to mean the towers that were built at the corners of the walls around cities in the kingdom of Judah. Those walls were not straight; they had angles and corners so that defenders could attack besieging armies from more than one direction. High towers were built at the corners so that the defenders could attack from a height.
עַל הֶעָרִים הַבְּצֻרוֹת וְעַל הַפִּנּוֹת הַגְּבֹהוֹת

The phrases fortified cities and high corners mean similar things. The high towers at the corners of city walls were one part of their fortifications. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
1:17: These words are similar to what the Lord said in Deuteronomy 28:29.

The point of this comparison is that just as a person who is blind does not know in what direction he should walk in order to arrive somewhere safely, so the Judeans will not be able to find any safe place to escape from the enemy army. The Lord is not saying that blindness is a punishment for sin.

The point of these comparisons is that just as people consider dust and dung to have no value, the blood and innards of the Judeans, vital to their lives, will be poured out as if those substances and the lives they sustain had no value.
1:18: The Lord is speaking as if the silver and the gold that the Judeans own were living things that could deliver them from their enemies.

The Lord is speaking as if his jealousy were a fire that is literally going to burn up the entire earth. As the next sentence indicates, he is using the term “earth” to mean the people who live on the earth, and he is referring to the way that he will punish those people for worshiping false gods and living sinfully. He is speaking of that punishment as if it were a fire.

Since the Lord does not kill righteous people along with wicked people, the word all may be a generalization for emphasis, or the expression the inhabitants of the earth may refer specifically to wicked people.
2:1: Zephaniah is implicitly telling the Judeans to Gather … together in order to repent. That is, he is telling them that they urgently need to hold a solemn assembly in which they confess and forsake their sins and ask the Lord to be merciful to them.

Zephaniah is expressing a positive meaning by using a negative word together with a word that is the opposite of the intended meaning. The phrase translated not desired could mean: (1) that the Lord does not want to be close to this nation because he is so angry with its people over their sinfulness and idolatry; (2) that the people of this nation are not ashamed of the wrong things that they have been doing.
Zephaniah is implicitly addressing the nation of Judah.
2:2: Zephaniah is referring implicitly to the decree of the Lord that he announced in the previous chapter.

The point of this comparison is that just as the wind blows away chaff so that it is gone and will not return, so the day of the Lord will come and go, and afterwards there will be no further opportunity for people to repent.
These two phrases mean similar things. Zephaniah is using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.

Zephaniah is using the term nose to mean anger. He is doing this by association with the way that a person who is angry breathes heavily through his nose. Zephaniah is also speaking as if the Lord’s nose or anger were literally burning. He means that the Lord’s anger is very intense.
Zephaniah is speaking as if the Lord’s nose, that is, his anger, were a living thing that could come upon the Judeans, that is, attack and overpower them.
2:3: Zephaniah is speaking as if he literally wanted the Judeans to Seek or look for the Lord.

Here the term earth could mean: (1) the land of Judah, since Zephaniah is addressing a specific “nation,” the nation of Judah, in verses 1–3; (2) the entire world, since that is what the term means in 1:18.

Zephaniah is speaking as if he literally wanted the Judeans to Seek or look for righteousness and humility. The meaning of this image is slightly different from its meaning in 1:6 and in the first part of the verse.
Zephaniah is speaking as if the Judeans could literally be hidden somewhere where the Lord could not find them.
2:4: For poetic effect and emphasis, at the beginning and end of this verse Zephaniah uses verbs that echo the sound of the names of the cities he is describing.
Zephaniah is speaking of the city of Ashdod as if it were a woman who could be expelled from the home in which she was living. He is using the city to represent the people who live in the city.

Zephaniah is speaking as if an army would literally expel the inhabitants of Ashdod at a specific time, at noon. He is likely using noon, the time when the sun is brightest in the sky, to mean “in broad daylight,” that is, as the result of an open attack by an overwhelming force.
Zephaniah is speaking as if the city of Ekron were literally a plant that could be uprooted, that is, pulled completely out of the ground, including its roots.
2:5: The word Kerethites is another name for all or part of the people group also known as the Philistines.
Zephaniah is using the term word to mean what the Lord has said by using words.
Zephaniah is speaking to something that he knows cannot hear him, the land of Canaan, in order to show in a strong way how he feels about the people who live there.
As Zephaniah did, the Lord is speaking to something that he knows cannot hear him, the land of Canaan, in order to show in a strong way how he feels about the people who live there.
2:7: Zephaniah is using the word house to mean the people who live in the kingdom of Judah.
Zephaniah is using one aspect of living in a house, lying down there in the evening (that is, sleeping there at night) to mean living there in general.

Zephaniah is using the term visit in a specific sense to mean taking action in regard to someone. In 1:8, 1:9, and 1:12, the term describes taking action to punish people. But here it describes taking action to help people.
2:8: The Lord is speaking of the country of Moab as if it were a living thing that could have expressed reproach against the people of Judah. He is referring to the people of that country.
Here the word sons means “descendants.” the Lord is describing the members of the Ammonite people group by reference to their common descent from a single ancestor, Benammi, here called Ammon.

This could mean: (1) that the Moabites and Ammonites have expanded their territories by taking territory away from the kingdom of Judah; (2) that the Moabites and Ammonites have threatened to attack the kingdom of Judah and take some or all of its territory.
2:9: The Lord is using this language to swear a solemn oath. He is indicating that the things he says will happen to Moab and Ammon are just as certain as some other very certain thing, the fact that he is alive.
The phrase The Lord of Armies is a title for God that indicates his great power. It describes him as the commander of heavenly armies.
מוֹאָב כִּסְדֹם תִּהְיֶה וּבְנֵי עַמּוֹן כַּעֲמֹרָה
The point of this comparison is that just as Sodom and Gomorrah were completely destroyed (see Genesis 19:1–29), so the countries of Moab and Ammon will be completely destroyed.
The Lord is speaking as if nettles and salt pits would literally own or possess the territory where the Moabites and Ammonites formerly lived.
שְׁאֵרִית עַמִּי יְבָזּוּם וְיֶתֶר גוי יִנְחָלוּם
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
2:10: The Lord is speaking as if the pride of the Moabites and Ammonites were literally an object that belonged to them. He is also speaking as if the destruction they are going to experience were also an object and as if he were going to take away their pride and give them destruction in its place.
2:11: Zephaniah is speaking as if the Lord is literally going to starve the false gods that other nations worship, that is, deny them food so that they become thin. This is likely a reference to the fat of animals that people sacrificed to gods. The implication is that people will no longer sacrifice to those gods because they will no longer worship them once the Lord has shown that he is the only true and powerful God.
Zephaniah is speaking of the nations of the world as if they were living things that could bow down to the Lord. He means that the people of the nations will do this.
The phrase a man refers to an individual. In this context it could mean an individual nation or an individual person.
2:12: The Lord is speaking as if he were literally going to pierce or kill the Cushites with a sword. He means that he is going to cause an enemy army to kill many of them.
2:13: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Zephaniah is using the term north by association to mean the empire that was located to the north of Judah, Assyria, as he indicates later in a parallel phrase.
2:14: The word translated columns refers specifically to the tops of columns, which often had ornate decorations. The implication is that an army will have destroyed the elaborate buildings of Nineveh so that only columns remain standing, and they are not supporting a roof, so their tops are exposed and provide a roosting place for birds.
Zephaniah is speaking of a bird’s call as if it were a living thing that could hoot on its own. He is using the call of birds to represent the birds themselves.
2:15: Zephaniah is speaking of the city of Nineveh as if it were a living thing that could exult, dwell in security, and speak. He means that the people of Nineveh have done these things.
כֹּל עוֹבֵר עָלֶיהָ יִשְׁרֹק יָנִיעַ יָדוֹ
Hissing and shaking a fist at Nineveh would be symbolic actions that expressed contempt for the city.
3:1: Zephaniah is implicitly referring to the city of Jerusalem.

As the introduction to this chapter discusses, here and through verse 5, Zephaniah is speaking of the city of Jerusalem as if it were a person who could be rebelling and who could have become defiled and who could be oppressing vulnerable people. Zephaniah is actually addressing the people of Jerusalem who have been doing these things.
3:2: The term voice could mean: (1) the voice of the Lord, that is, the message the Lord has been sending to the people of Jerusalem through his prophets telling the people to repent; (2) the voice of anyone who has been warning the people of the city that their wicked behavior will have destructive consequences.

Zephaniah is speaking as if the city of Jerusalem, meaning its people, could literally have drawn near to God, that is, moved closer to a place where God was. He means that they could have and should have worshiped God sincerely.
3:3: Zephaniah is speaking as if the princes of Jerusalem were literally roaring lions. He means that they exploit and harm vulnerable people rather than protecting them.

Zephaniah is speaking as if the judges of Jerusalem were literally wolves. As in the case of his comparison of the city’s princes to lions, he means that they exploit and harm vulnerable people rather than protecting them. By wolves of the evening, Zephaniah means wolves that have not eaten all day and so are especially aggressive from hunger.

Zephaniah is continuing to speak of the city’s judges as if they were wolves. The last thing a wolf would do in eating an animal it had killed, after consuming its flesh, would be to gnaw on its bones to get at the marrow inside. Zephaniah is saying that these judges are like wolves that eat an entire animal at once when they kill it in the evening or at night, leaving not even this final task for the morning.
3:4: Zephaniah is speaking as if the prophets in Jerusalem were literally light, that is, as if they did not weigh very much. He could mean: (1) that they are frivolous in character and so what they say is not profound or significant; (2) that nothing restrains them from doing wrong things, as if they were a light object with nothing weighing it down that would float away or be blown away.
3:5: בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר מִשְׁפָּטוֹ יִתֵּן לָאוֹר לֹא נֶעְדָּר

The word light could mean: (1) the light of dawn. In that case, Zephaniah would be saying the same thing twice in slightly different ways for emphasis. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. In that case, the phrase at light would apply to the first clause rather than to the second one.
Zephaniah is using the term morning to mean a day, by association with the way that each day begins with a morning.
3:6: הִכְרַתִּי גוֹיִם נָשַׁמּוּ פִּנּוֹתָם הֶחֱרַבְתִּי חוּצוֹתָם
The Lord is speaking as if he has done these things personally, but he means that the enemy army he has been describing throughout the book has done them.
These two phrases mean similar things. The Lord is using them together for emphasis.
3:7: The Lord is speaking to and about the city of Jerusalem as if it were a person who could fear him and take correction. He is actually speaking to and about the people who live in Jerusalem. See what you did in 3:1–5.

The Lord is using the expression rose early to mean that the people were eager to do corrupt things. The expression comes from the way that people get up early in the morning to do something if they are eager to do it.
The Lord says that as a generalization for emphasis.
3:8: לָכֵן חַכּוּ־לִי נְאֻם־יְהוָה לְיוֹם קוּמִי לְעַד

The imperative wait is plural, so the Lord is addressing some group of people. That group could be: (1) the wicked Judeans who are still disobeying the Lord despite his warnings. In that case, the Lord would be using the term wait to indicate that he is certainly going to do what he describes. In that case, the Lord would be using the term wait to tell them to be patient until he punishes sin and enforces justice.
While the Lord is going to punish sinful nations on a specific day, he is using that term here to refer to a specific time.
The Lord is speaking as if he were a predatory animal and the wicked nations and kingdoms that he is going to punish were prey that he was going to pounce on.

The phrase translated to the prey could also be translated as a witness. If that is the meaning, then the Lord would be speaking as if he were literally going to stand up and give evidence that these kingdoms and nations had sinned wickedly against him.
The Lord is speaking as if his indignation were a liquid that he was going to pour out onto wicked nations and kingdoms.
As the introduction to Zephaniah indicates, these parallel statements mark the boundaries between the major sections of the book.
3:9: The Lord is using the term lip by association to mean the capacity to speak. He could mean: (1) the peoples were saying wicked things because their character was wicked, but he will purify their character so that they will say pure things; (2) that by invoking the names of other gods (as described in 1:5), they had made themselves unworthy to pray to the Lord, but he will cleanse their capacity to speak so that they can pray to him.

Here, name represents a person by association with the way that each person has a name. However, in this instance there is also the idea that the peoples will call upon the Lord (that is, pray to him) by name, acknowledging him as God.
The Lord is using this expression to mean that the peoples will serve him unitedly, as if they were all putting their shoulders together to lift or push something heavy.
3:10: The Lord is using one distant place, the area around the rivers of Cush (the upper Nile region), to mean distant places in general.
Here the expression daughter of describes the people who make up a certain group. The group in view here is the Jewish nation that will have been scattered into many different places through exile.
3:12: The terms humble and lowly mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, name represents a person by association with the way that each person has a name.
3:13: וְלֹא־יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב וְלֹא־יִמָּצֵא בְּפִיהֶם לְשׁוֹן תַּרְמִית
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the word found indicates that something will not be able to be found because it will not be there.
The Lord is using the terms tongue and mouth by association to mean speaking.

The Lord is speaking as if the people in the remnant of Israel will be animals that will graze and lie down in pastures. He means that they will be able to live peacefully, like animals grazing undisturbed out in a field.
3:14: Here as well it describes the people who make up a certain group.
The word Zion is the name of the mountain on which the city of Jerusalem was located. Zephaniah is using the name by association to represent the entire kingdom of Judah, whose capital was Jerusalem.
The terms Rejoice and exult mean similar things. Zephaniah is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:15: It is true in one sense that The Lord is the king of the people of Israel. As their God, he is the ruler whom they must obey. But in another sense, he is not literally the king who rules from the palace in Jerusalem.
3:16: Zephaniah is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
These two phrases mean similar things. The people who are speaking to Zion are using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.
3:17: Since the people who are speaking to Jerusalem say that the Lord will rejoice and exult, they do not mean that he will literally be silent. Rather, they mean that the Lord will no longer speak words of condemnation and judgment against Jerusalem.
3:18: נוּגֵי מִמּוֹעֵד אָסַפְתִּי מִמֵּךְ הָיוּ מַשְׂאֵת עָלֶיהָ חֶרְפָּה
This verse is very difficult to understand. Modern versions translate it in many different ways.

The Lord may be using one kind of worship, a solemn assembly, to mean worship in general. He is addressing the city of Jerusalem as if it were an individual, so the phrase they are from you may be clarifying that the people who are grieving are Judeans who have been taken into exile and who are sad because they can no longer participate in the worship of the Lord.
The Lord is speaking as if the reproach of being conquered were literally a burden or heavy weight that Jerusalem was carrying with difficulty.
3:19: The expressions lame and cast-out one are both feminine singular, suggesting that the Lord is using both expressions to refer to Jerusalem as if that city were a female individual. In that case, the Lord would be using repetition to emphasize the idea that these phrases express. The reference would actually be to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, who would be lame or limping from the difficulty of walking from their homeland to a place of exile and who could be described as cast-out since they had been taken from their homeland.
The Lord is speaking as if he were literally going to turn the people of Judah into praise.
Here, name represents the reputation of a group.
3:20: The Lord is using the term eyes by association to mean sight.
